strings.tr_lede: Hum or sing one clear note at a time into your mic. It works for a single melody line — not chords. Steady “la-la-la” or “da-da” lands better than words.
strings.tr_hint: Tip: a hum lands roughly an octave below where a piano plays it. Turn off “Snap to key” to see the raw pitches, or pick the key to clean up stray notes. “Snap to beat” rounds the rhythm to your tempo so the values come out clean.
strings.tr_micfail: Couldn’t reach the microphone — allow mic access and try again.
strings.tr_none: No clear notes detected. Hum a bit louder and hold each note.
strings.ac_lede: Pick a progression and a playing pattern, then loop it at your tempo. The keys light up in rhythm — blue for the left hand, purple for the right — so you can play along. Set Hands to mute one part and play it yourself.

strings.greet_lede: Short, spaced sessions beat long cramming. A few minutes a day is all it takes.
strings.nextup_none: Nothing scheduled — explore freely or drill a topic.
strings.why_due: Spaced repetition schedules each idea just before you’d forget it — that’s when review sticks best.
strings.why_caught: Come back tomorrow and your reviews will be waiting — spacing is what turns practice into memory.

strings.pr_lede: Free practice on a single topic — it won’t change your review schedule, daily goal or streak, so grind as much as you like.

strings.ex_lede: Play anything — Étude names what you hold in real time. Open the Circle of fifths tab to hear any key’s scale or chord with fingering for both hands.
strings.ex_circle: Outer ring: major keys · inner ring: their relative minors. Click a key to hear it and see the fingering.
strings.songs_lede: Every interval, with famous tunes that open with it. Hum a song you know to lock in the sound. Click any title to hear the interval.
strings.method_intro: Étude isn’t a quiz — it’s built on what cognitive science actually says about learning a skill. Six ideas do the heavy lifting. None of them involve studying harder; they involve studying smarter.
strings.m1d: You remember something best when you review it right as you’re about to forget it. Each successful recall lets the next review wait a little longer.
strings.m1a: every concept carries its own due-date. Today shows what’s due; the schedule stretches as you succeed and snaps back when you slip.
strings.m2d: Pulling an answer out of memory strengthens it far more than putting it back in by re-reading. This is the “testing effect.”
strings.m2a: you always produce the answer — play the interval, build the chord, name what you hear — never just look at a chart.
strings.m3d: Mixing different problem types in one sitting feels harder than doing them in blocks — and that’s exactly why it builds more durable, flexible memory.
strings.m3a: a session shuffles intervals, chords, scales and progressions together, never two of a kind back to back.
strings.m4d: A little struggle is the signal that learning is happening. Effortless review barely moves the needle.
strings.m4a: once you can play a concept, it graduates to by ear — and the key changes every time, so you learn the idea, not one fingering.
strings.m5d: Fast correction stops errors from sticking, and a short “why” ties the new fact to things you already know.
strings.m5a: every answer is followed by the formula, a familiar-song hook, and how the sound feels — so it lands in context.
strings.m6d: The spacing effect: the same total practice spread across days beats one long cram. Short, frequent sessions win.
strings.m6a: a daily goal and streak keep it to a five-minute habit, and tomorrow’s reviews are always waiting.
strings.method_close: “We are what we repeatedly do.” The hard part of theory isn’t understanding it once — it’s remembering it under your fingers, months later. That’s the part Étude is for.

strings.an_limits: MusicXML (.musicxml, .xml or compressed .mxl) keeps the source notation. MIDI is rebuilt as notation on the rhythm grid you choose (1/16 by default); hands follow the MIDI tracks when they separate cleanly, otherwise a pitch split. A key signature in the file is kept; without one the key is estimated, and you can override it. A missing meter defaults to 4/4. Tempo changes are used for playback; repeats are not expanded. No PDF.
strings.an_desc: Open a MIDI or MusicXML file, or start with an example. Select notes to study keys, chords and harmony. Everything stays on this device.

strings.an_tip: Keys are estimated with duration-weighted Krumhansl–Kessler profiles, so a major key and its relative minor are told apart; the fit value r shows how clearly the notes match. Chords are matched beat by beat against chord templates weighted by duration, so passing notes lower the confidence instead of breaking the match. Roman numerals follow the written or chosen key. Click a chord or motif to select its notes.

strings.rd_lede: Learn to read music fluently: short drills for notes, intervals, chords, key signatures and rhythm, then sight-read real pieces. Use MIDI, the on-screen keys, or A–K.

strings.rd_done_learn: Done — %s slip(s). Run it again for a clean pass.
strings.rdx_ud_tr: From landmark notes to ledger lines — name, play and find every note of the treble staff.
strings.rdx_ud_ba: The left-hand staff, step by step: landmarks, lines, spaces and ledger lines.
strings.rdx_ud_gr: Both staves together, crossing middle C — the way piano music is written.
strings.rdx_ud_ac: Sharps, flats and naturals on the staff, then notes inside key signatures.
strings.rdx_ud_ks: Recognise major and relative minor keys from their key signature at a glance.
strings.rdx_ud_iv: Read the distance between two notes by shape, not by naming each note.
strings.rdx_ud_ch: Spot triads and their quality, then their inversions.
strings.rdx_ud_rh: Tap rhythms in time with the metronome; timing is graded to the millisecond.
strings.rdx_ud_cc: Alto and tenor clefs, for viola, cello and trombone parts.

strings.rdx_d_name: A note appears on the staff — choose its name as quickly as you can. Accuracy counts first, then speed.
strings.rdx_d_play: A note appears on the staff — play it on your MIDI keyboard, the on-screen keys or the computer keyboard (A–K). The exact octave counts with MIDI and the keys shown here.
strings.rdx_d_k2s: A key lights up on the keyboard — find the matching note on the staff among the options.
strings.rdx_d_iv: Two notes appear — name the interval between them (2nd to octave). Read the shape: line-to-line or space-to-space means an odd interval.
strings.rdx_d_ch: A three-note chord appears — name its root and quality. You can also play it.
strings.rdx_d_ks: A key signature appears — name the major key (its relative minor is shown under each answer).
strings.rdx_d_rh: Read a two-bar rhythm, listen to the count-in, then tap each note on the beat (Space, the TAP button or any key on your MIDI keyboard).
strings.rdx_d_sr: A new melody is written for you. Play it step by step (the score waits for you) or in time with the metronome for a score.
strings.rdx_p_k2s: Which note is the highlighted key?
strings.rdx_p_ks: Which major key has this key signature?
strings.rdx_keys_play: Play on MIDI, tap a key, or use A–K (Z/X octave)
strings.rdx_hint_odd: Both on lines or both in spaces → an odd interval (3rd, 5th, 7th)
strings.rdx_hint_even: One on a line, one in a space → an even interval (2nd, 4th, 6th, octave)
strings.rdx_hint_ks_s: Sharps: the major key is a half step above the last sharp
strings.rdx_hint_ks_f: Flats: the second-to-last flat names the key (one flat = F major)

strings.an_harm_note: Each chord lasts the whole bar unless the notes clearly change harmony on a beat, and is read from all the notes sounding in it, weighted by length and metric position. Exact: every chord tone sounds and no other reading comes close. Likely: the best fit, though a tone is missing, other notes sound or another reading comes close. Suggested: ambiguous; alternatives are shown. Non-chord tones are classified from their melodic approach, resolution and overlap with the next harmony.
strings.an_harm_implied: This passage is a single melodic line, so the chords are implied rather than played. They are estimated per bar or half bar and are only suggestions.
strings.an_harm_none: No clear chords in this passage.

strings.sym_dyn_ppp: pianississimo — as soft as possible; the quietest level
strings.sym_dyn_pp: pianissimo — very soft; much quieter than p
strings.sym_dyn_mp: mezzo piano — moderately soft; a little louder than p, softer than mf
strings.sym_dyn_mf: mezzo forte — moderately loud; a little louder than mp, softer than f
strings.sym_dyn_ff: fortissimo — very loud; much louder than f
strings.sym_dyn_fff: fortississimo — as loud as possible; the strongest level
strings.sym_dyn_sfz: sforzando — a sudden strong accent on this note, then back to the surrounding level
strings.sym_dyn_fz: forzando — a forced, sudden accent on this note only
strings.sym_dyn_rfz: rinforzando — a sudden reinforcement: this note or short group is suddenly louder
strings.sym_dyn_fp: forte-piano — attack loud, then drop at once to soft
strings.sym_cresc: Crescendo (hairpin <) — the volume grows gradually over the length of the wedge
strings.sym_dim: Diminuendo / decrescendo (hairpin >) — the volume fades gradually over the length of the wedge
strings.sym_t_dolce: dolce — sweetly, gently, with a soft warm tone
strings.sym_t_cantabile: cantabile — in a singing style; let the melody sing over the accompaniment
strings.sym_t_legato: legato — smoothly connected, no gaps between the notes
strings.sym_t_leggiero: leggiero — lightly, with a delicate touch
strings.sym_t_sostenuto: sostenuto — sustained; hold the notes their full length, often a little slower
strings.sym_t_rallentando: rallentando (rall.) — gradually slow down, relaxing the pace
strings.sym_t_atempo: a tempo — return to the main tempo
strings.sym_t_rubato: rubato — flexible time: stretch and push the tempo for expression
strings.sym_t_sim: simile (sim.) — continue in the same way (same pedalling, articulation or pattern)
strings.sym_t_larghetto: Larghetto — rather slow, a little faster than Largo
strings.sym_t_andantino: Andantino — a little faster than Andante
strings.sym_t_allegretto: Allegretto — fairly fast, lighter than Allegro
strings.sym_rehearsal: Rehearsal mark — a landmark letter for finding and starting from this place
strings.sym_ped: Ped. — press the sustain (damper) pedal; the notes keep sounding
strings.sym_pedup: * — release the sustain pedal; the dampers stop the sound
strings.sym_finger: Fingering — play this note with finger %s, the %b (1 thumb … 5 little finger)
strings.sym_finger_sub: Fingering — finger change on this note (%s): %b; start with the first finger, then switch while holding the key
strings.sym_staccato: Staccato (dot) — play the note short and detached
strings.sym_staccatissimo: Staccatissimo (wedge) — very short and sharply detached
strings.sym_accent: Accent (>) — play this note louder than its neighbours
strings.sym_marcato: Marcato / strong accent (^) — a strong, emphatic accent
strings.sym_tenuto: Tenuto (–) — hold the note its full value, gently stressed
strings.sym_fermata: Fermata — hold the note or rest longer than written, then continue
strings.sym_arpeggio: Arpeggio (wavy line) — roll the chord quickly from the bottom note to the top
strings.sym_trill: Trill (tr) — alternate rapidly between this note and the one above
strings.sym_mordent: Mordent — one quick alternation with the neighbouring note, then hold the main note
strings.sym_turn: Turn — ornament circling the note: upper note, main note, lower note, main note
strings.sym_slur: Slur — play the notes under the curve smoothly connected (legato), as one phrase
strings.sym_tie: Tie — join two notes of the same pitch: play once and hold for both values
strings.sym_gliss: Glissando / slide — slide from the first note to the second through the notes between
strings.sym_line: Voice-leading line — follow the melody as it passes from one hand to the other
strings.sym_clef_g: Treble clef (G clef) — the curl marks G above middle C on the second line; usually the right hand
strings.sym_clef_f: Bass clef (F clef) — the dots mark F below middle C on the fourth line; usually the left hand
strings.sym_clef_c: C clef — its centre marks middle C
strings.sym_key: Key signature — sharps or flats that hold for every note of that name until changed; here %s
strings.sym_time: Time signature — %s beats in each bar; the lower number (%b) gives the beat value
strings.sym_chord: Chord symbol — the harmony here: root, quality and, after a slash, the bass note

strings.rc_anchor: Find the first note from an anchor (Middle C or the clef’s line), then read the rest by direction: up, down or the same.
strings.rc_dir: Don’t name every note. First notice whether it rises, falls or repeats; then read the distance.
strings.rc_iv: After the first note, read the next one as a step, a third or a fifth instead of starting again: from one line to the next is a third.
strings.rc_chord: Stacked notes: read the bass first, then check whether the notes above sit a third or a fifth higher.
strings.rc_key: Check the key signature first (%a): it holds in every bar unless a natural cancels it.
strings.rc_hands: Two staves: read each beat from the bottom up — the left-hand note first, then the melody above it.
strings.rc_rhythm: Rhythm before pitch: feel the count-in bar, see where each note lands on the beat, and keep going after a slip.
strings.rc_ahead: Look ahead: while one note sounds, your eyes should already be on the next.
strings.rc_e_dir: Watch the direction: before each note, decide whether it goes up, down or stays the same.
strings.rc_e_dist: Right direction, wrong distance: count the lines and spaces — line to space is a step, line to the next line a third.
strings.rc_e_key: You played %a instead of %b: check the key signature and the accidentals before you play.
strings.rc_e_oct: Right note, wrong octave: check how far it sits from Middle C (Z / X move the computer keys by an octave).
strings.rc_e_chord: In the chords, read the bass first, then the notes stacked above it, and play them together.
strings.rn_clean: Clean read-through. Now try Assessment: the notes no longer wait for you.
strings.rn_again: Run it once more in Step by step and aim for no slips, then switch to Assessment.
strings.rn_dir: Direction slips (%a×): run it again and say “up”, “down” or “same” before each note.
strings.rn_dist: Distance slips (%a×): run it again and count the lines and spaces for every move.
strings.rn_key: %a instead of %b: name the sharps or flats of the key signature before you start, then run it again.
strings.rn_oct: Octave slips (%a×): find each note from Middle C before you play it.
strings.rn_chord: Most slips were in the chords: read each one from the bass up, then run it again.
strings.rn_a_top: Clean at a brisk tempo — pick the next piece.
strings.rn_a_good: Almost there: the same tempo again, with your eyes one note ahead of the cursor.
strings.rn_a_slow: Slow it to %a BPM and keep the beat going even after a slip.
strings.rn_a_learn: Learn the notes in Step by step first, then come back to Assessment.
strings.rn_a_leaps: Most misses were on the leaps: read them as thirds and fifths, not note by note, then try again.
strings.rn_a_chords: Most misses were in the chords: read them from the bass up and keep the beat.
strings.rn_a_acc: Most misses were on altered notes: check the key signature and the accidentals before you start.
strings.rn_a_extra: Extra notes (%a): play each note only when the cursor reaches it.
strings.rdc_land: Learn these landmarks cold: every other note is read as a step or two from the nearest one.
strings.rdc_tr: Read from a landmark, not from the bottom line: Middle %a, the %b on the clef’s line (2nd line) and the top-line %c.
strings.rdc_ba: Read from a landmark: the %a on the clef’s line (4th line), Middle %b just above the staff and the bottom-line %c.
strings.rdc_gr: Middle %a sits between the staves: one ledger line below the treble staff, one above the bass staff.
strings.rdc_lines: The lines, from the bottom up: %a.
strings.rdc_spaces: The spaces, from the bottom up: %a.
strings.rdc_ledger: Ledger lines continue the staff: count from the nearest staff line in thirds — line, line, line.
strings.rdc_acc: Read the sign before the note: ♯ is the next key up, ♭ the next key down, ♮ cancels.
strings.rdc_keys: Look at the key signature first: its sharps or flats apply to every note with the same name.
strings.rdc_play: Find the note from a landmark on the staff, then go to the same landmark on the keys and move from there.
strings.rdc_k2s: Name the key first, then find its line or space next to the nearest landmark.
strings.rdc_iv: Read the first note, then measure the second from it — a step, a third or a fifth — instead of naming it from scratch.
strings.rdc_ch: Read from the bass up: name the lowest note, then check that the others are stacked in thirds — all on lines or all in spaces.
strings.rdc_chinv: Inversions: if the notes are not all on lines or all in spaces, find the gap of a fourth — the root is its upper note.
strings.rdc_ks: Read the signature as a shape: count the sharps or flats, then apply the rule — no need to name each one.
strings.rdc_rh: Count one full bar before you start, and see where each note lands on the beat before you tap.
strings.rdc_cc: The middle of the C clef marks Middle %a: read every note from there.
strings.rdc_mix: Check the clef before every note: the same line is a different note in each clef.
strings.rdn_hints: Accuracy first: practise with auto-hints on, then take the test again.
strings.rdn_weak: Most misses: %a. Practise once more — missed notes come back more often.
strings.rdn_speed: Accurate but slow (%a s per answer; aim for %b s): Note rush trains reading speed.
strings.rdn_test: Ready for the test: 20 questions for up to three stars.
strings.rdn_star: For the next star: at least %a% right, under %b s per answer.
strings.rdn_rush: In Note rush a mistake costs 2 seconds: accuracy is the fastest way up.
strings.rdn_rh_low: Listen first, then tap: press Listen before each new rhythm and count along.
strings.rdn_rh_rush: You tend to rush (≈%a ms early): count the beats aloud and tap on them, not before.
strings.rdn_rh_drag: You tend to drag (≈%a ms late): look at the next note before its beat arrives.
strings.rdn_rh_ok: Steady timing — try a new rhythm or the next level.
strings.rdn_ok: Good session. Come back tomorrow: short, spaced practice sticks best.
strings.cn_nct: Non-chord tones here: %a (%b). They decorate the line; the harmony comes from the bass and the held notes.
strings.cn_nct_pass: Non-chord tones in these bars: %a. Read the harmony from the bass and the held notes, not from every quick note.
strings.cn_cad_auth: Authentic cadence (%a): the phrase comes home here — listen for the arrival.
strings.cn_cad_half: Half cadence (%a): the phrase pauses on the dominant and asks to go on.
strings.cn_cad_plagal: Plagal cadence (%a): the soft “amen” close, from the subdominant to the tonic.
strings.cn_cad_decept: Deceptive cadence (%a): the dominant resolves somewhere unexpected — the phrase is not over.
strings.cn_sec: %a is a secondary dominant (%b): its raised note leans into the next chord.
strings.cn_inv: The bass is %a, not the root: read the chord from the bottom up — %b.
strings.cn_amb: The harmony is ambiguous here (%a): trust the bass and the longest notes over the quick ones.
strings.cn_implied: A single melodic line: the chord (%a) is implied by the notes on the strong beats.
strings.cn_T: Tonic (%a): home. Notice which melody notes belong to the chord and which pass between them.
strings.cn_S: Subdominant (%a): the music moves away from home, often on its way to the dominant.
strings.cn_D: Dominant (%a): tension that wants to resolve to the tonic — listen for the leading tone.
strings.cn_chr: Chromatic chord (%a): a note from outside the key colours this moment.
strings.cn_key: These bars lean toward %a (the piece is in %b): look for the accidentals that take it there.
strings.cn_bass: Follow the bass line: where it moves, the harmony usually changes.
strings.cn_fall: Look a beat ahead at the notes coming down, not at the keyboard.
strings.pn_clean_tempo: Clean at %a. Next: one notch faster.
strings.pn_clean_hands: Clean with one hand. Next: both hands together.
strings.pn_clean_wait: Clean with Wait for me. Next: play it in time.
strings.pn_clean: Clean run! Once more without looking at your hands, eyes a beat ahead.
strings.pn_bars: Most slips were in %a: loop just that spot until it is clean.
strings.pn_wait: Missed notes (%a): turn on Wait for me and take the time to read each one.
strings.pn_wrong: Wrong keys (%a): practise one hand alone first, then put them together.
strings.pn_loose: Many notes were a little off the beat: keep your eyes a beat ahead of the blue line.
strings.pn_loose_fall: Many notes were a little off the beat: look a beat ahead at the falling notes, not at the keyboard.
strings.pn_slower: Try it slower: accuracy first, speed later.
strings.pn_ok: Good run: repeat it at this tempo until it is clean, then speed up.

keys.b:
Music uses just 12 different notes. After the twelfth, the pattern starts over — the same note, higher up. That distance is an octave, and the piano is simply the same 12-key pattern repeated over and over.

The white keys are named C D E F G A B (Do Re Mi Fa Sol La Si). The black keys sit between them and borrow their names: the black key above C is C♯ (“C sharp”); the same key seen from D is D♭ (“D flat”). One key, two names — that’s called enharmonic spelling.

Half steps & whole steps

From any key to its closest neighbour (black or white) is a half step (semitone) — the smallest distance we use. Two half steps make a whole step. Notice that E–F and B–C have no black key between them: those are natural half steps, and they’re what gives every scale its shape.

To find any C: look for the group of two black keys — C is the white key just to their left. Middle C (C4) sits closest to the centre of the piano.

iv.b:
An interval is the distance between two notes, counted in half steps. Every melody and every chord is built from them — learn to hear intervals and you can pull songs out of the air.

Each interval has a size (2nd, 3rd, 5th…) and a quality (major, minor, perfect). Play them all from C:

Consonance & dissonance

Octaves, 5ths, 4ths, 3rds and 6ths sound stable (consonant). 2nds, 7ths and the tritone sound tense (dissonant) — they want to move somewhere. Music breathes by moving between the two.

The fastest way to memorise intervals is to anchor each one to a song you know — a major 6th is the start of “My Bonnie”. Browse the interval song book, then drill them by ear.

sc.b:
A scale is a ladder of whole (W) and half (H) steps. The pattern is what matters — start it on any note and you get the same flavour, just higher or lower. The major scale is the sound of “Do Re Mi”:

W · W · H · W · W · W · H

The natural minor scale rearranges the same steps for a darker mood: W · H · W · W · H · W · W. Every major scale hides a minor one that uses exactly the same notes, starting from its 6th degree — A minor is the relative minor of C major.

So what is a “key”?

Saying a song is “in C major” means the C major scale is its home base: its notes feel right, and the note C feels like home. The sharps or flats that scale needs are written once at the start of the staff — the key signature.

Pentatonic scales drop the two “spicy” degrees (4 and 7) — five notes that sound good in almost any order, which is why they’re everywhere from folk to rock solos. Drill scales →

ch.b:
A chord is three or more notes sounding together. The basic unit is the triad: a root, a third and a fifth — built by skipping every other scale note. Its two building blocks are just intervals stacked:

  • Major — 4 + 3 half steps · bright, resolved
  • Minor — 3 + 4 · darker, melancholy
  • Diminished — 3 + 3 · tense, unstable
  • Augmented — 4 + 4 · dreamlike

Beyond the triad

Add one more third and you get 7th chords — the sound of jazz, soul and gospel. Swap the third for its neighbour and you get floating sus chords.

Inversions

The same notes in a different order are still the same chord. Put E or G at the bottom of C major and you have an inversion — smoother to reach, same identity.

Hold any chord in Explore and Étude names it live — inversions included. Drill chords →

cof.b:
Line up the 12 keys so each step is a perfect 5th and they close into a circle: C → G → D → A… all the way back to C. This is the circle of fifths — the subway map of harmony.

Why it matters:

  • Key signatures: each step clockwise adds one sharp (G has 1, D has 2…); each step counter-clockwise adds one flat.
  • Neighbouring diatonic scales (major or natural minor) share 6 of 7 notes. Harmonic and melodic minor alter notes and can change that count; moving one step is generally one of the smoothest key changes.
  • Chord movement by 5ths feels inevitable — the V → I cadence, the jazz ii–V–I, and the endless “circle” progressions all walk this wheel.

The interactive circle lives in Explore › Circle of fifths — click any key to hear its scale or chord, see the fingering for both hands and set the Roman-numeral context.

pr.b:
Build a triad on each degree of the major scale, using only that scale’s notes, and you get the diatonic chords — the palette of a key. We label them with Roman numerals so the pattern works in every key: uppercase = major, lowercase = minor, ° = diminished.

IiiiiiIVVvivii°

Chords have jobs

  • Home (tonic): I and vi — rest, arrival.
  • Away (subdominant): IV and ii — motion, lift.
  • Tension (dominant): V and vii° — they pull hard back to I. The V→I move is the cadence, music’s full stop.

A progression is a loop through those jobs. A handful of them power most songs you know:

Loop any of these with left-hand patterns in Accompany, or drill them →

rh.b:
Rhythm has two layers: a steady beat (what you tap your foot to) and the pattern of longer and shorter notes riding on top. Beats group into bars; the grouping is the meter, written as a time signature.

  • 4/4 four beats per bar — pop, rock, almost everything. ONE two three four…
  • 3/4 three per bar — the waltz. ONE two three…
  • 6/8 six quick eighths felt as two big beats — a lilting, rolling feel.

Note values

Each note value lasts half as long as the one before: whole (4 beats) → half (2) → quarter (1) → eighth (½) → sixteenth (¼). A dot adds half the note’s own length again — a dotted half = 3 beats.

Tempo is the speed of the beat, in beats per minute (BPM): 60 = one per second; 120 = twice as fast.

The sight-singing exercises start with long notes and add faster values level by level.

notation.b:
Written music is a graph: time flows left to right, pitch runs up and down. Notes sit on a grid of five lines — the staff. Every line and every space is one letter name; move up one position and the name moves up one letter.

Two clefs, one keyboard

The treble clef (𝄞) marks the staff for higher notes — usually the right hand. Its curl wraps the G4 line. The bass clef (𝄢) is for lower notes — the left hand — and its two dots hug the F3 line. Middle C sits exactly between the two staves, on its own little ledger line.

Read patterns, not letters

Good readers don’t spell out every note — they read intervals on the page: line to the next line (or space to space) is a 3rd; line to the neighbouring space is a 2nd. Learn a few anchor notes and step from them.

Ledger lines, accidentals & the key signature

Notes above or below the staff ride on short ledger lines. A ♯ or ♭ written before a note lasts to the end of that bar. The cluster of sharps or flats at the very start — the key signature — applies to the whole piece and names its key.

Put it into practice in Read & play — step-by-step mode waits for the right key, then Assessment scores you against the beat.

dyn.b:
The notes tell you what to play; the markings around them tell you how. These are what turn typing into music.

Dynamics — how loud

  • pp pianissimo — very soft · p piano — soft · mp mezzo-piano — medium soft
  • mf mezzo-forte — medium loud · f forte — loud · ff fortissimo — very loud
  • crescendo (hairpin <) — gradually louder · diminuendo (>) — gradually softer

Articulation — how notes touch

  • Legato (a slur arc over notes) — smooth and connected; one finger releases as the next lands.
  • Staccato (a dot) — short and detached; bounce off the key.
  • Accent (>) — lean into the note. Tenuto (–) — hold its full value, slightly weighted.
  • A tie joins two notes of the same pitch into one longer note; a fermata (𝄐) holds a note beyond the beat.

On a piano, dynamics come from key speed. Étude’s synth responds to MIDI velocity — try the same chord soft, then hard, in Explore and listen to the colour change, not just the volume.

modes.b:
Start the major-scale pattern from a different rung and you get a mode — the same notes with a different home, and a completely different colour. Two you already know: Ionian is the major scale, Aeolian the natural minor.

  • Dorian — minor with a bright 6th; folk and jazz, “Scarborough Fair”.
  • Phrygian — minor with a dark ♭2; flamenco, film villains, metal.
  • Lydian — major with a floating ♯4; dreams and film scores.
  • Mixolydian — major with a relaxed ♭7; rock, blues, bagpipes.
  • Locrian — built on a ♭5, unstable; rare and spiky.

Hear them from the same root and the colours pop: Mixolydian vs. major — only the 7th changes. Dorian vs. minor — only the 6th.

Drill the modes by ear →

how.b:
Theory sticks when it moves through your ears and hands, not just your eyes. Étude’s whole design follows a few rules you can use anywhere:

  • Recall, don’t reread. Always try to produce the answer — play it, sing it, name it — before you peek.
  • Anchor sounds to songs. Every interval hides at the start of a tune you already know.
  • Sing everything. If you can sing a third, you own it. Humming counts.
  • All keys, small doses. Ideas, not fingerings: a chord you only know in C is a quarter of a chord.
  • Daily beats weekly. Five minutes a day outruns an hour on Sunday — that’s the spacing effect.

The science behind this is in Method. When you’re ready: today’s session →

symbols.t: Road signs: repeats, codas, pedal & ornaments
symbols.b:
Composers save paper with navigation marks — they tell you where to jump instead of writing music out twice. Read them before you start playing, like checking a map.

Repeats & jumps

  • 𝄆 … 𝄇 Repeat signs — play the section between them twice. If there is no start sign, go back to the beginning. 1st / 2nd endings (brackets over bars) change only the last bar(s) of the repeat.
  • D.C. (da capo, “from the head”) — go back to the very beginning. D.S. (dal segno) — go back to the sign 𝄋.
  • al Fine — then stop at the word Fine (“end”). al Coda — play until “To Coda”, then jump to the coda 𝄌, the closing tail.

Pedal, fingering & ornaments

  • Ped. … ✱ or a bracket line — hold the sustain (right) pedal, then lift. Change pedal with each new harmony so chords don’t smear.
  • Fingering numbers — 1 is the thumb, 5 the little finger, in both hands. Small numbers above or below notes are suggestions that save you from running out of fingers.
  • Ornaments decorate a note: tr trill (rapid alternation with the note above), mordent (one quick flick to the neighbour and back), turn (𝆗 — above, note, below, note), grace note (a tiny note crushed in just before the beat).

Before playing a new piece, trace its road map with your finger: where are the repeats, where does D.C. send you, where is Fine? Most “wrong notes” in a first run-through are actually wrong turns.

rh2.b:
Silence is part of rhythm. Every note value has a matching rest of the same length — count rests exactly as firmly as notes.

Dots & ties

A dot adds half the value: a dotted quarter = 1½ beats, usually followed by an eighth to finish the beat. A tie (a curve joining two notes of the same pitch) glues them into one sound — the only way to hold a note across a bar line. Don’t confuse it with a slur, which joins different pitches and means legato.

Triplets & syncopation

A triplet squeezes three notes into the time of two — a “3” over the group. Syncopation puts the accent where you don’t expect it: on an off-beat, often a note that starts between beats and is held through the next one. It’s the lifeblood of ragtime, jazz, funk and pop.

Compound meter

In 6/8, 9/8 and 12/8 the beat is a dotted quarter that splits into three eighths: ONE-and-a TWO-and-a. Simple meters (2/4, 3/4, 4/4) split each beat into two.

Tempo words

Largo (very slow) · Adagio (slow) · Andante (walking) · Moderato · Allegro (fast, lively) · Presto (very fast). Changes: rit./rall. slow down gradually, accel. speed up, a tempo back to the original speed, rubato flexible, breathing time.

Count out loud — “1-and-2-and”, “1-trip-let 2-trip-let” — while you tap. Saying the subdivision is what makes syncopation land in the right place.

iv2.b:
An interval has two names: the number (count letter names, both ends included: C up to E = C-D-E = a 3rd) and the quality (count half steps). The number comes from the page; the quality from the keyboard.

  • Perfect intervals — unison, 4th, 5th, octave. Make them one half step bigger → augmented; smaller → diminished.
  • Major/minor intervals — 2nd, 3rd, 6th, 7th. Major minus a half step = minor; minor minus another = diminished; major plus one = augmented.

So the same key distance can have two spellings: F–B is an augmented 4th, B–F a diminished 5th — both are the 6-half-step tritone. C–E♭ (minor 3rd) and C–D♯ (augmented 2nd) sound identical, but they mean different things in a key.

Inversion — flip it over

Move the bottom note up an octave and the interval inverts. The numbers always add to 9, and the qualities swap: major ↔ minor, augmented ↔ diminished, perfect stays perfect. A major 3rd (C–E) inverts to a minor 6th (E–C).

Compound intervals

Intervals larger than an octave are compound: subtract 7 to find the simple interval. A 9th is an octave + a 2nd, a 10th an octave + a 3rd. Jazz chord names (9, 11, 13) use these numbers.

Quick check for any interval: count letters for the number, then compare with the major scale of the bottom note — if the top note is in that scale, the interval is major or perfect.

minor.b:
Every scale step has a name and a job. Learn the names once and you can talk about any key:

1 tonic2 supertonic3 mediant4 subdominant5 dominant6 submediant7 leading tone

The leading tone sits a half step below the tonic and pulls up into it. When the 7th is a whole step below (as in natural minor) it’s called the subtonic — and that pull disappears.

Three minors

  • Natural minor W H W W H W W — the relative minor, same notes as its major.
  • Harmonic minor — raise the 7th (G → G♯ in A minor). Now V is a major chord with a real leading tone. The gap between 6 and 7 is an exotic augmented 2nd (W+H).
  • Melodic minor — raise 6 and 7 going up, to smooth that gap; classical style returns to natural minor coming down.

Relative & parallel

Relative keys share a key signature (C major / A minor — the minor tonic is 3 half steps below). Parallel keys share a tonic (C major / C minor). Composers borrow freely between both.

Build any of these with the scale builder in Scales & keys: start from natural minor, then move the last steps.

ch7.t: Seventh chords, colour chords & slash chords
ch7.b:
Stack a fourth note — a 7th above the root — and the chord gains colour and direction. Five seventh chords cover almost all music:

  • maj7 (major triad + major 7th) — soft, lush: the I and IV chords in jazz and bossa.
  • 7 (major triad + minor 7th) — the dominant seventh, tension that wants to resolve: V7.
  • m7 (minor triad + minor 7th) — mellow: ii7, vi7.
  • m7♭5 (diminished triad + minor 7th), “half-diminished” ø — the ii of a minor key.
  • dim7 (diminished triad + diminished 7th) — all minor 3rds, maximum suspense: vii°7 in minor.

Colour chords

sus2 / sus4 replace the 3rd with the 2nd or 4th — neither major nor minor, open and floating. 6 adds the 6th to a major triad (a warm, old-fashioned ending). add9 adds the 9th without the 7th — the sparkle of countless pop ballads.

Slash chords

C/E means “C chord over an E bass”. It may be an inversion (E is in the chord) or a different bass entirely, like C/B♭ or F/G (a soft dominant). Slash chords let the bass walk smoothly: C – C/B – Am – Am/G – F.

Try every quality and slash bass with the chord builder in Chords. Lead sheets write exactly these symbols over the melody.

cad.b:
A cadence is the chord move that ends a phrase. Like punctuation, some end the sentence and some leave it hanging:

  • Perfect authentic (PAC) — V(7) → I, both in root position, melody ending on the tonic. A full stop.
  • Imperfect authentic (IAC) — V → I but weaker: an inversion, or the melody ends on 3 or 5. A semicolon.
  • Half cadence (HC) — any chord → V. A comma or question mark: “to be continued”.
  • Plagal (PC) — IV → I, the “Amen” ending of hymns.
  • Deceptive (DC) — V → vi. You expect home and get a surprise; the phrase must go on.

Find them in real music

The Minuet in G ends its first half with a half cadence and its second with a PAC — open Score & Analysis to see the Roman numerals under each bar.

Listen for cadences in any song: hum the last chord of each line. Does it feel finished (authentic), hanging (half) or surprised (deceptive)?

minorh.b:
Build triads on natural minor and you get iii°IIIivvVIVII. But a minor v has no leading tone, so composers almost always borrow the raised 7th from harmonic minor — the dominant becomes major: V (E major in A minor), and vii° gets its pull back.

Common minor progressions

  • i – iv – V – i — the classical backbone.
  • i – VI – III – VII — the epic pop/film loop (Am – F – C – G).
  • i – VII – VI – V — the “Andalusian cadence”, a stepwise descent heard from flamenco to rock.

Für Elise

Beethoven’s famous opening is pure A minor: the right hand swings between i (A–C–E) and V (E–G♯–B) — listen for the G♯, the borrowed leading tone.

Write Roman numerals in minor with lowercase for minor chords (i, iv) and uppercase for major (III, V, VI, VII) — the case tells you the borrowed notes at a glance.

nct.b:
Melodies don’t only use chord notes. Notes that clash with the harmony for a moment — non-chord tones — create motion and expression. They are named by how they’re approached and left:

  • Passing tone (P) — fills the gap between two chord tones by step, in one direction.
  • Neighbour tone (N) — steps away from a chord tone and back to the same note.
  • Suspension (S) — a chord tone is held (tied) into the next chord, clashes, then resolves down by step: the classic 4–3.
  • Appoggiatura (App) — leaps onto a dissonance on a strong beat, then resolves by step. The “sigh”.
  • Anticipation (A) — arrives early: the next chord’s note sounds just before that chord.

In Für Elise

The opening E–D♯–E is a lower neighbour figure: D♯ is not in the harmony, it just decorates E. Look for P and N labels in the analysis view.

To analyse a melody note: is it in the chord? If not, check its neighbours — how did it arrive (step or leap) and where does it go?

secdom.b:
Any major or minor chord in a key can get its own dominant. In C major, the V of G is D major (D–F♯–A): we write it V/V, “five of five”. The borrowed F♯ acts as a temporary leading tone pulling to G — a moment of colour without leaving the key.

Modulation

When the new tonic sticks — confirmed by a cadence in the new key — you’ve modulated. The smoothest route is through a pivot chord that belongs to both keys: Am is vi in C and ii in G, so C – Am – D7 – G slides into G major. Most classical pieces modulate to the dominant (major) or the relative major (minor) and come home at the end.

Voice leading

Think of each chord as 3–4 singers. Good voice leading moves each singer as little as possible:

  • Keep common tones in the same voice; move the others by step.
  • Resolve tendency tones: the leading tone (7) goes up to 1; the 7th of a chord goes down by step.
  • Avoid parallel 5ths and octaves between two voices — they make the voices merge into one.
  • The bass may leap; the upper voices prefer steps.

On the piano, voice leading is also a technique tip: inversions keep your hand in one place. Compare the two demos above — same chords, very different effort.

form.b:
Music is built like language: small ideas combine into sentences, sentences into paragraphs.

  • Motif — the smallest recognisable idea, a few notes (Beethoven’s Fifth: short-short-short-long). It returns, transposed and varied.
  • Phrase — a musical sentence, usually 4 bars, ending in a cadence.
  • Period — two phrases as question and answer: the antecedent ends open (half cadence), the consequent starts the same way and ends closed (authentic cadence).

Larger forms

Label sections with letters; a repeated section keeps its letter, a varied one gets a prime (A′).

  • Binary (AB) — two halves, each often repeated. Typical of Baroque dances like the Minuet in G.
  • Ternary (ABA) — statement, contrast, return. Minuet + Trio + Minuet; many songs and nocturnes.
  • Rondo (ABACA…) — a refrain that keeps coming back between episodes; Für Elise is a small rondo (A B A C A).
  • Verse–chorus — pop’s version of the same idea, often with an intro, bridge and outro.

When learning a piece, mark its sections first. Knowing that bars 9–16 are just A again can halve your practice time.

accomp.b:
A lead sheet gives you only the melody and chord symbols (C, Am7, G/B…). Turning it into piano music means choosing a left-hand pattern — the same chords can sound like a waltz, a ballad or a march.

  • Block chords — the whole chord on the beat; simplest, strongest.
  • Broken chord / arpeggio — the chord notes one after another; flowing.
  • Alberti bass — low–high–middle–high (C–G–E–G): the sound of Mozart and Clementi.
  • Waltz — bass on 1, chord on 2 and 3. Boom-chick — bass on 1 and 3, chord on 2 and 4 (ragtime, stride, country).
  • Pop ballad — bass + a slowly unfolding chord, with the sustain pedal changed on each chord.

From lead sheet to piano

  1. Play the chord roots in the left hand while you sing or play the melody.
  2. Add full chords in the left hand, using inversions to stay close (voice leading!).
  3. Choose a pattern that suits the style and metre; keep the melody on top in the right hand.
  4. Read slash chords literally: the note after “/” goes in the bass.

All these patterns — with any progression and tempo — loop in Accompany.
